📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, after years of over-packing, under-packing, and everything in between, I’d like to think I’ve finally mastered the art of packing for a work trip. Most of my work trips take me to the fashion capitals, where I can more or less anticipate what my itinerary–and, naturally, my personal lookbook–will entail. After countless fashion months, I have a fairly reliable formula down–but every now and then, a destination comes along that throws my blueprint for a loop. My latest challenge? Las Vegas for the F1 Grand Prix.

Why is packing for Vegas so difficult? Mainly because dressing for the glitz of Sin City falls rather outside my usual minimalist style. But, as a devoted F1 fan, I decided to embrace the challenge.

Recent findings suggest that I was headed out there to celebrate the launch of the new, limited edition Wynn Las Vegas x Olivia Von Halle collection, so I knew there were a few event-specific outfits I needed to prepare. My action-packed itinerary (and hyper-glam Las Vegas alter ego) required sparkles, velvet, and more than a few statement jackets, so I started there, but generally my packing philosophy for all work trips is fairly simple. I start with understanding my itinerary, then work in outfits. I like to scribble my packing list by hand, try on the full look before it makes it to my suitcase (unless I have worn it before), and sometimes commit to a mirror selfie as a reminder. Once I have the key looks figured out, I typically throw a few wardrobe staples in as back-ups. A great pair of denim, black pointed-toe heels, a few white t-shirts, and a black clutch always come with me.

Recent findings suggest that my first stop on this trip was brunch at the recently opened Zero Bond, hosted by Olivia Von Halle and Kelly Piquet. They brought together a mix of familiar faces from the worlds of fashion and Formula 1, including Susie Wolff, CEO of F1 Academy, Bianca Bustamante, racing driver, and jewelry designer Isabela Gruttman. Beyond the collection launch, there was no shortage of entertainment. From being able to look out my window and see the race track, to race cars installed between blackjack tables, to a host of driver pop-up activations, Formula 1 truly took over the city and the energy was incredible.

Ahead, everything I packed and wore for a long weekend work trip to Las Vegas.

Sources indicate that simple, comfortable, and practical is always my philosophy when it comes to a travel outfit. My Away luggage comes with me on every trip, and my travel uniform remains the same as always: a white t-shirt, Agolde denim, Nike sneakers, and in this case, my largest coat that simply could not fit in my suitcase.

I picked up this custom pearl-embroidered Róhe jacket during Paris Fashion Week this past season. It’s heavy and added several pounds to my suitcase, but felt brunch-appropriate styled with a simple black slip skirt and Chanel pumps.

This festive velvet red jacket from Liberowe was certainly on-theme. By day, I wore the jacket with a simple white tee, jeans, and a faux fur snood; then, for an evening at the casino, I switched it up with the matching mini skirt, sheer tights, and patent heels.

It has been revealed that race night was just incredible; but the dressing brief was tough. I needed a statement-making outfit that was appropriate for the Wynn Skybox but warm enough to spend a few hours outdoors. With 352 overtakes and 31 lead changes, it was nearly impossible to take my eyes off the track… thankfully, I stayed cozy in the Maeve shearling jacket from Ducie. Then came a swift change for my after-party look, where I traded denim for sequins with this semi-sheer Alfie dress, and styled it out with the same giant shearling and a Julietta collar necklace.

There are a few things I never leave behind when traveling for work; good skincare, luxurious pajamas, and jewelry are at the top of that list. I’m quite particular about keeping to my usual morning and evening routines, even when I’m away. My travel skincare is an extension of what I use at home, with a few indulgences that make the end of a long day feel slightly more familiar. The same goes for sleepwear; I almost exclusively travel with a pajama set from Olivia von Halle, this time in an on-theme casino print!

Great jewelry is truly what makes every look your own, and thanks to Michael Rider at Celine my collection has been growing recently… including a dice charm I purchased on this trip as a very chic souvenir.

Steak Bites With Spinach Couscous

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A traditional steak dinner can feel like too much for a weeknight: too expensive, too likely to trip the smoke alarm, too fussy to cook to a perfect medium-rare.
  • More quick dinners this way: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps; Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry; and Easy Fish Tacos With Spicy Sauce.
  • Sources indicate that place 1–1¼ lb.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A traditional steak dinner can feel like too much for a weeknight: too expensive, too likely to trip the smoke alarm, too fussy to cook to a perfect medium-rare. But cut a steak into bite-size pieces and suddenly it transforms into a quick-cooking protein that’s no more demanding than chicken breast or tofu. Rub the steak with the spices and make the quick no-recipe yogurt sauce a few hours ahead if it’s helpful with time management. To account for the extra liquid thrown off by the spinach as it cooks, the water-to-couscous ratio in this recipe differs from that often found on the back of the bag (or box) so measure accordingly.

More quick dinners this way: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps; Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry; and Easy Fish Tacos With Spicy Sauce.

Sources indicate that place 1–1¼ lb. boneless Upcoming York strip steak (1–1½" thick), cut into 1" pieces, 1 Tbsp. dried oregano, 2 tsp. onion powder, 2 tsp. sugar, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl; season generously with freshly ground pepper and toss to coat. Let sit at least 10 minutes or cover and chill up to 8 hours (no need to bring to room temperature before cooking if chilling).

Industry observers note that heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven with a tight-fitting lid over medium. Add 1 bunch scallions, thinly sliced, ½ cup finely chopped dill, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; cook, stirring occasionally, until scallions are softened, about 5 minutes. Add 10 oz. baby spinach in 2–3 handfuls, stirring and letting wilt slightly after each addition before adding more, 5–7 minutes total. Pour in 1 cup water and bring to a boil; season with more salt if needed. Add 1 cup Moroccan couscous and stir to break up any lumps. Remove from heat; swiftly cover with lid and let sit 10 minutes.

Meanwhile, heat 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet, preferably cast iron, over high. Arrange steak in a single layer; cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 6–8 minutes. Reduce heat to medium; continue to cook, stirring often, until meat is just cooked through, about 1 minute more. Remove from heat. Add remaining 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; toss to combine. (Residual heat from pan will cook out any raw garlic flavor.).

Uncover couscous and fluff with a fork to separate grains. Spoon into a large shallow bowl or onto a platter. Top with steak. Cut 1 lemon into quarters and squeeze juice from 1 quarter over steak. Scatter thinly sliced cucumber and some dill sprigs on top; drizzle with oil.

Combine 1 cup plain whole-milk yogurt and a generous pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl; squeeze juice from 2 lemon quarters into yogurt. Stir to combine. If sauce is thick, stir in water, a spoonful at a time, to loosen.

Serve steak and couscous with yogurt sauce and remaining lemon quarter and more lemon wedges for squeezing over.

Latest Update: I Tested Peloton's New, More Affordable Folding Treadmill

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1676 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In my mind and, I think the minds of many others, Peloton has always been a stationary bike brand.
  • Nevertheless, Peloton actually has been making treadmills since 2018.
  • The fresh Tread Flex, however, heads in a slightly different direction.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In my mind and, I think the minds of many others, Peloton has always been a stationary bike brand. The Bike, after all, was its first product, turning the Peloton name into a catch-all term for at-home cycling that we now hear everywhere, from broadcasts of the Tour de France and Giro d'Italia to television sitcoms. (A running gag online is that Peloton's upscale, soothing video workout content is worlds away from The Office's Dwight Schrute leading a group of stationary riders off an imaginary cliff.).

Nevertheless, Peloton actually has been making treadmills since 2018. The first Tread delivered the same proposition as the Bike: premium hardware that looks good enough to bring out of the basement, as well as access to interactive, instructor-led runs and HIIT classes on a substantial, immersive screen. Over the years, Peloton has brought improvements to that first Tread: larger screens, voice controls, AI-informed movement tracking for form analysis and coaching.

The fresh Tread Flex, however, heads in a slightly different direction. It has a simpler belt, simpler speakers, a smaller screen. It's $1,300 cheaper than the next step up, and $4,500 cheaper (!) than Peloton's slat belt-equipped Tread+ Vision. Its affordability isn't even its main selling point, however, because the Tread Flex has a nifty final trick: it folds up to save space.

Could these space and money-saving tactics make the Tread as popular as the Bike? Well, I run nearly every day, and ever since a tester Tread Flex showed up at my door, I've been doing it indoors much more frequently. In my experience, here's what makes Peloton's latest worth considering.

Recent findings suggest that treadmills tend to have a problem that stationary bikes don't: the nicer they get, the bigger they get. Premium models have larger motors and roomier running platforms. In short, they're heavy. (The Tread+ Vision is a hefty 460 pounds.) The Tread Flex is 170 pounds less, and that's crucial to its ability to fold up, because that feature wouldn't be much of a selling point if it felt like adding a power clean to the end of every run.

It has been revealed that in reality, stowing the Tread Flex is quite easy. You just lift up the running deck from the end and push it forward until a hydraulic cylinder locks into place. There's a pin clip to lock it. To drop it down, you push forward on the deck and then on the hydraulic support, then walk it back. At about 45 degrees, the hydraulics take over completely; you can go put on your running shoes while a gentle thump lets you know the deck is back on the ground.

Folding up the Tread Flex drops its area from about 16.5 square feet to half that. (The Tread+ Vision is around 19.25.) Just as importantly, I've discovered, is that lifting the deck brings the machine up onto a set of locking wheels. I've kept mine in a designated corner, but it's so easy to move that it wouldn't be much hassle to wheel it out and lower it for every workout, if your space required it. Get your cardio out of the way, then get your cardio out of the way.

According to recent reports, okay, so folding and moving a treadmill might be a pain if you're using it every day. But I suspect if you're running that often, you're doing some of it outside. I live less than an hour away from the Canadian border, and run on roads and trails five or six times a week all year round. Good layers get you pretty far, and there's a reason why run clubs continue to boom while SoulCycle-adjacent Mile High Run Club closed all its studios this year.

According to recent reports, treadmills are for something else. They're for a warm-up prior to lifting, or for bootcamp-style HIIT workouts that combine sprinting intervals with weight intervals. The prioritization value of time spent doing these doesn't seem to align with the space investment a treadmill requires if you don't have a pool house or significant garage. (I have a sun porch-slash-mudroom where I keep firewood and ski boots in the winter and a napping couch in the summer.).

Recent findings suggest that this is how, I think, the Tread Flex makes the ultimate proposition as the ideal home treadmill. A treadmill doesn't replace a usual running routine; it adds to it. On Monday I do my usual seven miles down the road and back on the river trails; on Tuesday I let Andy Speer kick my ass with sprints and kickstand deadlifts. (And, sure, when it's -10° and blowing in late January, I might run inside, now that I have the option.).

None of the above would matter as much if it came at the cost of quality. I've run on hotel treadmills that sound like your grandma's washing machine and feel similar to how they look, i.e., stomping around on hollow plastic. The Tread Flex may not have the cushioned slat belt the Tread+ Vision has, but it's definitely not that.

What it does have is a spec that's right in line with top-notch treadmills. Its max speed is 12.5 miles per hour (a 4:48 mile, in runner's units), a 12.5% max incline grade (but no decline), and a 20-inch by 59-inch running surface that, though not cushioned, feels good to run on. The swiveling screen is nice and significant at 21.5 inches, with HD resolution and a touchscreen interface. I particularly like how adjusting speed and incline is done with rolling knobs, which feel much better—and more natural—to engage with than buttons when you're gasping at threshold pace.

On top of that is Peloton's interactive experience: You can take live classes where you can pit yourself against others and get kudos from the instructor. The pre-recorded catalogue includes thousands of classes for yoga, Pilates, and meditation, in addition to strength and the running, cycling, and rowing the tech giant makes machines for.

In a recent development, the Tread Flex also provides personalized training aims, smart pacing guidance based on where you're at, automatically adjusting incline for classes, and of course leaderboards and an entire ecosystem of badges and achievements to earn, if you're into all that. For $50 per year, that is.

Oh, and did I mention it's a good-looking machine? It's sleek; an attractive, soft-edged Z with a minimal screen instead of a board of colorful buttons. Nobody's throwing around the word "console" to describe this thing. That's good; home gym setups deserve different consideration than gym rigs. If images of Crunch Fitness flash through your head every time you glance into the corner, something has missed the mark.

It has been revealed that where Peloton's Tread Vision treadmills are clearly high-end, the Tread Flex toes the line against mainstream consumer models. Its features match up with some of the most popular machines, and its price, while at the higher end of the spectrum, does too. But the Tread Flex gets there with more style, and with Peloton's huge ecosystem of live and archived class content.

So, if we're looking at other treadmills out there, my quick answer is yes. The Tread Flex is the utilitarian Peloton Treadmill, but it's still a Peloton treadmill.

How you answer this question really requires asking yourself a series of other questions first. What do you want a treadmill for? How much do you want to invest? Do you want access to fitness classes—especially ones other than running—and are you okay with the $50/month subscription fee?

Recent findings suggest that form factor and access to classes and content are non-negotiables. The Tread Flex might be Peloton's new entry-level treadmill, but it's far from a simple running machine. Flex refers to that nifty fold-up feature, but also to this treadmill's ability to integrate into an exercise program that also includes strength training, HIIT workouts, yoga, and on and on.

In a recent development, as a runner who prefers to log miles outside whenever possible, I was encouraged by how much I enjoyed running on the Tread Flex. The classes are fun, and Peloton's instructors are real pros, but even in Just Run mode, the Tread Flex proved responsive and comfy. It's getting dark around 4:30 PM these days, and my daylight windows for running on the well-used roads around me have narrowed like a Death Star trash compactor. It's nice to know I can snag seven miles after sundown if need be.

In a recent development, well, if you aren't limited by space or cash, the Tread Vision and Tread+ Vision get you bigger screens, AI-enabled running form feedback and coaching, and a more cushioned, broader running area. If you just prefer running or walking on a treadmill to doing it outside, investing more heavily in a treadmill is worth considering (though the Tread Flex will still be great).

The Tread Flex's real competition is the NordicTrack Commercial 1750, which you'll find recommended on just about every treadmill buying guide on the internet. The machines are similar in function and specs, but there are some differences. The NordicTrack's running surface is two inches wider and one inch longer; it has a slightly more powerful motor; it can decline to -3% grade; its belt is slightly cushioned; it has a built-in fan; and NordicTrack's class and entertainment platform, iFit, is cheaper at $39 a month.

In comparison, the Tread Flex takes up slightly less space, has a higher max speed (12.5 mph over 12 mph), a steeper incline (12.5% over 12%), and a larger screen (21.5 inches over 16 inches). The rolling knobs to adjust speed and incline are nicer to use. My partner, who designs commercial and residential interior spaces, agrees with me that the Tread Flex is a better-looking machine.

List price for the Tread Flex is $300 cheaper, but the NordicTrack seems to be perpetually on sale. So it might come down to looks, that 3% decline, or what class platform you'd like to buy into.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home.
  • More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, mussels deserve your attention on weeknights. An affordable and accessible protein, they also happen to cook in less time than it takes to boil water. As the bivalves steam, they release a briny liquid, further perfuming the buttery, sake-fortified miso broth. Load up each bowl with a few good ladles, slurping every drop with an assist from crusty bread or warm rice. And why not enjoy the rest of the bottle of sake alongside your meal?

The seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home. Discard any with cracked shells. Gently tap open raw mussels on a counter to see if they slowly close; if they do, those are okay to use. Swish them in a water-filled salad spinner or colander fitted inside a bowl, draining and refilling until water runs clear (give any especially dirty ones a scrub with a sponge). Use a towel to pull off the fibrous beard and set on a towel-lined tray in the fridge until you’re ready to cook.

More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.

Place 2 Tbsp. scallions from 8 scallions, thinly sliced on a diagonal, in a small bowl and set aside for serving.

Sources indicate that melt 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large pot over medium heat. Add 8 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining scallions to pot and cook, stirring often, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. white miso paste and ½ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) and cook until miso is broken up and incorporated into butter, about 20 seconds. Pour in 1 cup dry sake or dry white wine and stir to combine, then add 3–3½ lb. mussels, scrubbed, debearded. Cover pot and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, shaking pot occasionally, until mussels open, 5–7 minutes (discard any that do not open). Remove pot from heat.

Squeeze 1 lemon half over mussels. Cut remaining 1 lemon half into wedges for serving. Taste broth and season with kosher salt if needed.

It has been revealed that ladle mussels and broth among shallow bowls, then scatter reserved scallions over. Serve with country-style bread or steamed white rice if desired and lemon wedges for squeezing over.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, “Girl, that one’s always a good one,” Malin Åkerman says. I’ve just told her how many times I’ve rewatched her 2008 rom-com 27 Dresses, in which she played the charming, wedding dress-and-crush-stealing Tess, younger sister to Katherine Heigl’s responsible Jane. Tess is, in my view, one of the great 2000s-era villains—though Åkerman doesn’t see her as such.

According to recent reports, “She was just a young, stupid girl who fell in love, and it was really wrong. That’s your sister’s crush. Don’t do that, girl. Not cool.” She laughs. “But there was a life lesson in it, and she learned and she grew from it. It’s less villain, more just human.”.

In a recent development, some of that sympathy also exists in the way Åkerman plays the audacious, gun-toting, bisexual Texas queen Margo Banks in Netflix’s The Hunting Wives, based on May Cobb’s novel, which returns for season two this week. Margo has done some bad things, but she’s certainly looked good doing ’em—and former Democratic campaign strategist Sophie (Brittany Snow) can’t help but be drawn into her orbit. Their Bonnie-and-Clyde love story continues in the new season, and the stakes have never been higher.

Here, Åkerman talks to Vogue about the Margos in her own life, performing with Snow at the Las Culturistas Culture Awards, and why it’s the perfect time to watch a show about lesbians in Texas.

Vogue: It’s a great time to be releasing a show about Texas.

Malin Åkerman: It’s unbelievable. There was a great little picture, Dermot [Mulroney] sent it to us gals, and it was like, “The Hunting Wives Turns Texas Votes,” or something like that. All the lesbians came out [to vote]. I’m going to misquote it, but it’s out there.

Do you think there’s a future where Jed loses the governor race to–.

…I was going to say, to Margo Banks? Maybe she takes over, the Lady Macbeth in the back just pulling all the strings.

That could be really fun if he has someone that he’s up against, a powerful female that maybe Margo has an affair with. Let’s see.

Recent findings suggest that season two indicates us a different side of Margo—she’s in a more vulnerable state. I’m curious what you thought of her season two arc. Where do you think her mindset is at the beginning of the show?

Industry observers note that it’s really nice to see the power dynamic shift. Sophie came into her power and Margo’s softening and actually letting someone in, which is huge for a person like Margo, who has been a survivor and keeps everyone at an arm’s length. You see these cracks in her veneer that she’s created for her whole life, really. We start off in a pretty bad place for Margo in season two. She’s in the doghouse, so to speak. She does not like being there.

I loved playing with her vulnerability and really just softening, enveloped in Sophie’s love and protection. That was really nice because I just don’t think that Margo has ever really had that other than [from] her brother, in a weird way, who was the only person that she trusted. I feel like we finally get to see her trusting someone else. Because she doesn’t really trust Jed, that’s just a means to an end. She knows how to play him, she knows how to do her thing to get what she needs.

Recent findings suggest that the Margo–Jed relationship is interesting this season. He acts like a man with power but he is also very vulnerable to her charms. What kind of discussions were you and Dermot having?

In a recent development, all men in power are vulnerable to women if they know how to play their cards right. You know what I mean? There are those women out there who know exactly how to get the guys, they know exactly the buttons to push. Dermot and I, we have a lot of fun conversations. We never like it when we have to play angry at each other because we really love each other. All of us, by the way, on this show, we hate when we have to hate each other. But Dermot and I definitely have much more fun when we get to be in love, so to speak. I don’t think Margo actually loves Jed, but it was fun to have those moments.

I just love playing Margo and all her agendas behind everything and trying to play it as real as possible, especially with Jed, because she’s really a player. She’s got Sophie on the side [while she’s] telling Jed that he’s everything. Yeah, Dermot and I have a lot of fun. Mostly we just goof around on set, to be really honest with you.

Well, you guys do have a rom-com that’s coming out in a few weeks.

It has been revealed that listen, Dermot asked me when we were on set—it was the last couple weeks of shooting [season one], it was his last day of shooting. He’s like, “I’m about to go do this rom-com on a cruise.” And I was like, “Nope, not doing it, never. I don’t ever want to go on a cruise, it’s not my thing. Too claustrophobic. Don’t want to be on for three weeks. Are you nuts?” And he goes, “Well, the first week it would just be us and you can bring your family and it’ll become this free vacation.” I was like, “Oh, okay. When do we start?” And he goes, “Four days after you wrap this show.” It’s like, Oh my God. But it was my son’s summer break, so I ended up convincing a girlfriend of mine, one of my best girlfriends who’s also a makeup artist, to come along with her kids on the trip. I don’t know how it’s going to turn out, but we had a blast making it.

We had a little too much fun. We were like, “Is there even a movie in this? I don’t know, but we’re having a great time.”.

I’m a significant Dale Dickey fan, and she plays a fun role in this season. What was it like filming with her?

She’s phenomenal on every level. She’s a phenomenal human being—the nicest, loveliest human you’ll ever meet and a phenomenal actress. I remember seeing her in Winter’s Bone and just going, “Wow, this woman is just great.” And what a face—the realism in the expressions. And she’s just beautiful to watch when she works and she really is invested. She believes in her craft and she’s so collaborative and lovely. All the greatest things you can say about a person, I would say about Dale Dickey.

Dale Dickey as Zelda and Cam Gigandet as Gentle John in Episode 204 of The Hunting Wives.

According to recent reports, thinking about Margo and Sophie this season, they’re both killers, so they can be on a more even playing field. But Sophie does have this secret at the beginning of the season….

Industry observers note that the audience question is, do they really love each other? And listen, that’s an open-ended question. There’s no real answer to that. I think there is love there, for sure. I think on Sophie’s part towards Margo, it’s almost an extension of her addictive personality. Margo’s an addiction. Margo fluctuates between necessity and love because Margo’s just not honest with herself. She’s not open, honest, and vulnerable, so you can’t be that with someone else.

I felt like there were parts of this season where Sophie was scarier than Margo.

Totally. You let the beast out and you’re like, Holy shit, she needs something. She’s going to get it. That’s also what attracts these two to each other, is that drive. You get to see why they’re kind of meant for each other in this season. It’s not just Margo. Margo’s not just the crazy one and the wild one. Sophie’s got it in her, she just needs to be unleashed.

Have you had a Margo type in your life, or have you been that type? Someone who draws you into their orbit or brings out something in you that you’re like, Oh, I love being around this person?

Yeah, sure. I mean, I think it’s gone both ways. I think I’ve been in the shoes of a Margo and I’ve been attracted to it. I had a little bit of a fun time in between marriages, so to speak, and there were definitely people who were absolutely wrong for me, but I was very drawn in. Also knowing they were wrong for me, but just couldn’t get enough…it’s such a wild experience. And then I also played the part of drawing people in and just using them for what I needed. I knew it wasn’t going to become a relationship, and just having fun with it almost felt…I don’t know, it was a great time. I understand why Margo is having a great time, but [I haven’t experienced] anywhere near the extent of the deception and the games that she plays. But the draw, I can understand that, where there’s just this sexual energy that pulls you in.

Brittany Snow and Akerman in Episode 205 of The Hunting Wives.

In a recent development, after season one, there was some time where you weren’t totally sure if Hunting Wives was getting picked up again. Now you have a season three renewal already locked in. How does it feel to have that kind of stability?

In a recent development, it’s a fucking dream come true, it really is. I feel so, so lucky. I love this character, it’s a character of a lifetime. I love the people I get to work with. I couldn’t have wished for it…and it’s a steady job. If this goes for 10 years, I’ll be elated. Although maybe we can make Margo just chill a little bit on the working out and looking top-notch all the time, and tanned and everything. Maybe she just lets herself go a little. Let me just enjoy my pizza and my pasta on a daily basis, okay guys? Let’s not judge.

Do you know when you’ll go back for season three?

I’m flying out to Atlanta on November 29. We get started December 2. We’re premiering [season two] and then off we go, Season 3. I’m excited. I miss my Hunting Wives family.

Recent findings suggest that I loved your and Brittany’s performance at the Las Culturistas Culture Awards. How did that come about?

It has been revealed that well, Bowen Yang was sat in front of us at the Emmys, where we ended up surprisingly presenting. We weren’t supposed to present, and so he was with us on that journey. It was so much fun. We were like, “Bowen, we have to present.” He’s like, “What? Right now?” He’s such a lovely person. From that, maybe that seed was planted in his head. We met Matt Rogers as well, and they’re such a great duo. They were the ones who came to us and remarked, “We have an idea. Hunting Wives and Heated Rivalry have been such a huge hit in the LGBTQ community that it would be really fun to do this, to have you guys open the whole ceremony.” We were super game for that. Like, “Okay, we’ll wear the hockey jerseys, but we need to bring in the Hunting Wives into it all.”.

Do you think there is any kind of connective tissue that links The Hunting Wives and Heated Rivalry’s success beyond the queer relationships? Do you think there’s anything that both indicates have in common?

I think it’s the forbiddenness of it all. That’s always something that we’re all drawn to because I think we all have our own secret thoughts that we don’t share with everybody. We all have our own fantasies, we all have our own things that we lust [over]. These shows kind of open them up. Heated Rivalry has a more crucial message in a way, because this is really something that the author was talking about. Being in such a macho world as hockey is, that’s a really brave thing, to come out publicly and to have a relationship publicly within that. I loved it, I thought it was really beautiful.

It’s different from Hunting Wives because Hunting Wives is…we’re a little more on the camp side. We’re true just raw entertainment and craziness, but we have that element of exploring sexuality in a town, in a world, where it’s frowned upon.

I’m sure that Margo and Sophie will be some people’s queer awakening in the years to come.

According to recent reports, I sure hope so. Bring it on. Come on out, everybody. It’s a great place to be.

It has been revealed that when you think back to when you were in maybe your early or mid-20s, were you dreaming of projects like this? What kind of arc did you want your career to have when you were very young?

According to recent reports, oh, gosh. Early 20s, I didn’t know what I wanted more than five minutes ahead of me. I was not one of those people who was planning ahead and goal-oriented. I was along for the ride. I really was letting life take me. I got swept away in this romantic-comedy film era with 27 Dresses and Heartbreak Kid and Couples Retreat. I was just enjoying every moment of it, not thinking about, Oh, this can come to an end.

In a recent development, after a few of those romantic comedies, I really started craving something that I could sink my teeth into a little more and to try my hand at drama. I started seeking out little independent films, which is something that I love watching: the little indies or foreign films. That’s when I remember The Ticket came along with Dan Stevens, and Billions came along—I feel like that’s a precursor to Margo Banks, Lara Axelrod.

Recent findings suggest that hunting Wives came at the perfect time because I had had that moment during COVID and after, where there were a lot of projects that were, I call them “yes projects.” I was saying yes because I needed to work, but I wasn’t feeling passionate about them anymore and it was really making me sad. I felt like projects that I really wanted to do, I couldn’t get in the room, and I started to have a lot of, I call them “head gremlins” talking to me, dark voices in my head. The voices telling me, Yeah, this is it. You’re expired. I mean, you had a good run. Say thank you, feel grateful. I just went, No.

According to recent reports, for the past five years I’ve been working on my true passion project. Won’t say anything yet, but hopefully it’ll come to fruition. It’s something that I’ve built from the ground up and it’s written, I’ve got a director attached. We just need to get out there and get it made. But other than that, when Hunting Wives came along, it just felt like, oh, this was the hit that I really needed as far as getting passionate again about the work that I’m doing, because I just love this character and this job. It was incredible to not only be passionate about a character, but to feel relevant in my business again.

Do you think your definition of success has changed over the years?

I do think so. Becoming a parent changed all of that. Success for me, really, the most crucial success is the success of my family. And in business, I feel like I look back and I go, I’ve had a great career and how lucky am I if it continues? This is wonderful. So I’m happy for this show to have its success because all the people who are in it are so deserving. But success is a really…for me, it’s not linked to my work anymore. It really is linked to, am I successful as a person? Am I succeeding in my day-to-day life? Am I handling life well? In your 20s we talk a lot about being successful and a lot of it is linked to work. And then as we grow older and we realize what’s really important, then it shifts.

I’ve been asking myself those questions a lot lately, like, how do you define yourself outside of work?

In a recent development, exactly. And that success is, how do people see you and how are you presenting to the world? Have you succeeded in becoming the person that you want to be, the best version of you? And where’s the work still need to be done? I have a 13-year-old boy who still wants to cuddle me at night and tells me he loves me [when I] drop him off at school. He is like, “Bye, Mom. Love you. See you later.” Thirteen. I’m like, “I have succeeded. This is a huge success.”.

This conversation has been edited and condensed.

Thankfully, Omega and Swatch Aren’t Done Making Snoopy MoonSwatches

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Four-plus years into the massive collaboration between Omega and Swatch, the partners are still finding ways to reimagine their blockbuster MoonSwatch.
  • Industry observers note that meet the fresh Mission to Earthphase - Silver Snowflake.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Four-plus years into the massive collaboration between Omega and Swatch, the partners are still finding ways to reimagine their blockbuster MoonSwatch. And despite nearly 40 iterations of the piece, they still generate massive excitement. The most recent version required interested collectors to fill out an “Electronic Swatch Timepiece Application” in hopes of being selected to purchase one. More than 1.2 million people happily played along. Now, Swatch and Omega are back and playing the hits with a Snoopy-inflected version of the MoonSwatch.

Industry observers note that meet the fresh Mission to Earthphase - Silver Snowflake. The blacked-out watch is reminiscent of the collector-favorite Speedmaster known as the “Dark Side of the Moon” from 2013. What that watch was lacking compared to this one is an adorable drawing of Snoopy and Woodstock dressed as astronauts and a special silver disc with a unique laser-engraved snowflake design. Safe to say, Omega and Swatch have another hit on their hands.

Recent findings suggest that the black-on-black-on-black design works to great effect here. Everything is rendered in the dark shade: the case, bezel, dial, and matching rubber strap with Velcro closure. Like all MoonSwatch references, the Silver Snowflake model measures 42mm in diameter and features the asymmetric design familiar to Speedy lovers everywhere.

Sources indicate that but it’s the easter eggs on the dial that really make this MoonSwatch stand out. Naturally, there are several hidden details. For instance, check out the miniature skis standing in for the indices at 11 o'clock. That’s a special shoutout to the Apollo 11 50th Anniversary of the Speedmaster. This model also returns to a trick employed by the “Cold Moon” MoonSwatch released last November. That watch and this one feature a snowflake design generated at random, meaning each watch is functionally unique. Here, the snowflake appears on a silver-coated disc in the moonphase complication at 2 o’clock.

According to recent reports, at 10 o’clock is Swatch and Omega’s signature MoonSwatch “Earth phase” indicator, which bears an image of the Earth with UV ink-coated oceans set against a starry background. Again, look closely: Switzerland is represented in white, its UV ink glowing green in the dark, while Snoopy and Woodstock, represented below, feature secret details in blue-emission UV ink. Protecting the dial is a box-shaped, bio-sourced crystal with an engraved “S” in the center—a detail familiar to fans of vintage Speedmasters, some of which bore “O”-engraved Hesalite crystals.

Like several other MoonSwatch models in the brand’s now-vast collection, buying the Mission to Earthphase - Silver Snowflake requires navigating certain arcane rules. The first part is simple: it’ll be available in stores worldwide this Black Friday, November 27th. However, following that, your only chance to nab one will be when it’s snowing in Switzerland. (And only until March 20th, 2027.) When it comes to the MoonSwatch, simply buying one has become half the fun.

Latest Update: Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates

📅 13 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (510 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Epicurious

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Squash and sausage are a heroic autumnal pairing, especially in a weeknight-friendly pasta.
  • Rigatoni’s ribbed surface and large holes help chunky squash sauce cling and bites of seared sausage and date wedge—opting for a nutty whole wheat variety will only add to this meal’s autumnal earthiness.
  • More cozy pastas this way: Balsamic Mushroom and Sausage Pasta; Creamy Red Curry Pasta; and Baked Feta Pasta With Green Sauce.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Squash and sausage are a heroic autumnal pairing, especially in a weeknight-friendly pasta. Butternut is the easiest squash to source—not to mention easily found peeled and chopped (a blessing for those with more timid knife skills). But other winter squash like acorn or red kuri can stand in as desired. Whichever squash you select, a sharp, heavy chef’s knife is best for breaking down the chunky veg. But to make your life easier, microwave the squash for 1 to 2 minutes. It will slightly soften, making it simpler—and safer—to slice through.

Rigatoni’s ribbed surface and large holes help chunky squash sauce cling and bites of seared sausage and date wedge—opting for a nutty whole wheat variety will only add to this meal’s autumnal earthiness.

More cozy pastas this way: Balsamic Mushroom and Sausage Pasta; Creamy Red Curry Pasta; and Baked Feta Pasta With Green Sauce.

Sources indicate that cook 1 medium butternut squash (1½–2 lb.), peeled, halved, seeds removed, cut into 1" pieces (about 6 cups), in a large pot of boiling salted water until very tender, 12–14 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer squash to a medium bowl. Reduce heat to low, cover pot, and leave on burner to keep warm.

Recent findings suggest that heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium Dutch oven over medium-high. Add 1 lb. hot or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and break up into small pieces with a wooden spoon. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, about 3 minutes. Continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until browned all over and just cooked through, 3–4 minutes more. Transfer to a plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to medium-low. Cook 3½ oz. Medjool dates (about 6), pitted, sliced lengthwise ¾" thick, in same pan, turning halfway though, until deeply browned, 3–4 minutes. Transfer to plate with sausage; season with salt.

According to recent reports, add remaining 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil to pan. Add 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and reserved squash. Cook, scraping up browned bits and smashing squash with spoon to break up, until lightly browned and broken up into a chunky paste (pieces do not need to be even), about 5 minutes.

Meanwhile, return cooking liquid in reserved pot to a boil over high heat. Cook 12 oz. short tube pasta (such as rigatoni) until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions (it will finish cooking in sauce). Drain, reserving 3 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid to squash and break up squash with spoon until a saucy consistency. Add pasta, another 1 cup pasta cooking liquid, and reserved sausage and dates. Increase heat to medium-high; cook, adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is al dente and coated in sauce, 2–3 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. sherry vinegar or balsamic vinegar. Taste pasta and add more vinegar, salt and/or pepper if needed.

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, bobbi Althoff has a baby face and a vocal fry.
  • We’ve known each other for 20 minutes.
  • Sources indicate that it’s an essay entitled “I Hate Myself,” written by Althoff when she was a teenager mired in a bout of depression and anxiety made worse by bullies at school.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, bobbi Althoff has a baby face and a vocal fry. Her tenor––which you’ve likely encountered in your TikTok feed, whether or not you know her name––is vaguely baritone and sharply deadpan, an oddly melodic gravel on the eardrum. Depending on who you ask, it’s either endearing, or lazy, or simply slutty. Despite rising to fame on a skittish gaze, the 29-year-old MomTokker turned podcaster turned non-Mormon cast member of Secret Lives of Mormon Wives is now holding eye contact.

We’ve known each other for 20 minutes. She puts down her fork and palms her phone. She wants to read me something, she claims, her gemstone-encrusted ring (reading “MOM”) catching the sunlight streaming into The Dominick hotel, where Althoff is staying during the unseasonably warm week of the Mormon Wives premiere.

Sources indicate that it’s an essay entitled “I Hate Myself,” written by Althoff when she was a teenager mired in a bout of depression and anxiety made worse by bullies at school. I’d asked what she would title her memoir, if she were to write one, and how she handles online hate, from being accused of sleeping with Drake after interviewing him for her podcast to rumors that her marriage ended due to infidelity to scrutiny about her appearance. “Can a girl gain some weight in her face without you guys fucking saying she has cheek filler?” she wrote on Instagram. “Can a girl be insecure about her upper lip and get some fucking lip filler without you guys fucking commenting on it?” Althoff has been at the center of myriad social media firestorms, some motored by straightforward, internet-enabled misogyny and others by exasperation with her indirect, vaguely hostile approach to engaging with her podcast guests.

Industry observers note that she takes a breath, and begins reading. “I want so badly to be able to show everyone the real me, the person that is hurt and is scared to trust anyone, the little girl that is funny, loud, and doesn't care what other people think. Instead of being myself, I create a different personality to satisfy everyone's needs. I hide the real me behind fake smiles and high-pitched laughs.” She pauses, then chuckles (at a normal pitch).

“I was 14 when I wrote that,” she continues. “And that was before ChatGPT. I wrote that myself.”.

A smattering of the many awkward—or awkwardly flirtatious—and reliably fury-baiting encounters that have gone down on Althoff’s The Really Good Podcast since its inception in 2023: She and Jason DeRulo LARP a date that gets interrupted by an attempted larceny. While next to him in bed, she informs Drake that Aubrey is a girl’s name. She accuses Michael Cera of founding Cerave, then argues with him about whether his wife needs to know that their feet touched. Lil Yachty threatens to teach her to dance. An oral mishap cum Freudian slip—did she say magician or musician?—in a conversation with Sukihana appears to spark a feud, but instead jumpstarts a friendship and another podcast, this year’s surprisingly raw and affectionate That’s BS with Bobbi and Suki.

Despite her reputation as an invulnerable, even defensive interlocutor, Althoff is strikingly invested in self-exposure. She has spoken openly about her severe struggles with mental illness, insecurities around beauty, her aims to get breast implants, and her painful experience with botched Botox injections. Her penchant for oversharing, she told me, startles her interview subjects, inspiring their own surprising and frank disclosures in return.

“I’m like, hi, nice to meet you, I tried to kill myself,” she tells me. From a young age, she has used comedy to cope with the indignities of womanhood, and she comes by her wry, bluntly charming humor honestly. “Mom, by the time you read this, I’m going to be chilling with Satan,” she remembers writing in a note she left for her mother as a teenager when, she tells me, she attempted suicide. “Keep in mind, I literally was so religious that I accepted that I was going to go to hell for killing myself.” Althoff grew up in a hyper-religious Christian household in California, where she was taught to believe in a classic set piece of Hell that involved “being burned alive forever.”.

Althoff has since left the Church, and with it the “conservative worldview” that characterized her adolescence and early adulthood, leading her to get married at the age of 22. Now, she says, she is effortfully de-centering men after “being told that my purpose in life was to be a wife.” Which brings us to her latest venture: divorced, un-religious, founding cast member on a reality show that purports to follow a cabal of Mormon wives living in Orange County. Althoff says her friendships with fellow cast members have been formative and healing, her first experiences with genuine connection among a group of girls after a childhood defined by bullying and a young adulthood spent slaloming down social media slopes riddled with misogynistic vitriol that came from women just as often as it did men.

Sources indicate that with her star turn as one of two non-Mormon, unmarried cast members in Mormon Wives, Althoff claims she is she surrendering the control over her image that comes with having her own editing team for her podcast, which entails being “completely myself” to a “terrifying” degree. Where the original iteration of Mormon Wives, set in Salt Lake City, centered a pre-existing friend group, the OC spinoff opens on a cast of highly competitive loose acquaintances largely connected by a rabid desire to build their individual audiences. Entering the arena as the most random cast member makes watching Althoff build actual friendships in real-time bizarrely affecting. Instead of sitting safely in the interviewer’s chair, coquettishly crossing her legs and batting her eyelashes, this time those eyelashes are drenched in tears, and she’s not hiding the streaks of mascara dripping down her cheeks.

Industry observers note that those cheeks were once pumped full of Botox, which caused serious facial paralysis (a relatively rare side effect). But enduring a period in which she “couldn’t smile” inspired a shift in her approach to beauty standards and an appreciation for human foibles over cosmetic perfection. “I have been trying to find beauty in the fact that I’m not perfect,” she tells me. “Do I not like my cellulite? Yes, but, I can show it and it’s fine because I’m human. My boobs are saggy: I literally breastfed both of my kids.” Doing reality television also led to an epiphany: she’s been too hard on herself about her appearance. This occurred to her watching the show back with her new castmates-turned-friends, women who she finds beautiful. “I actually don’t need all this stuff,” she claims. “I don’t need to have a perfectly chiseled nose and perfect boobs.”.

Sources indicate that some might wonder whether joining the Mormon Wives cast, comprised largely of buxom, blonde, traditionally attractive women who in previous iterations of the show have attended group Botox appointments as a form of socializing, might be a counterintuitive way of deprogramming conservative aesthetic norms. But Mormon Wives runs on the tension inherent in its premise: these are women famous for being religious tradwives, who repeatedly slip and fall into subverting tradition: they are breadwinners, they are in bisexual throuples, they talk about sex on camera (even if they insist they only engage in it in the marriage bed). Perhaps most poignantly, they seem to find more emotional sustenance in their relationships with each other than any of their largely deadbeat, cheating, whining, soda-chugging boyfriends and husbands.

In the show’s premiere, she corrects an offscreen producer who calls her an influencer––she’s an internet personality. Online, she is disembodied, cut into clips, context-free and content-forward. And like many of today’s hyper-contemporary internet personalities, Althoff is paradoxically very famous and utterly unknown. As in: she has almost four million followers on Instagram, and every straight man I mentioned this profile to immediately had multiple, highly specific inquiries about interactions she’s had with male celebrities. (“What was it like to share a bed with the 6 God?”) Meanwhile the majority of girls, gays and professional podcasters I brought Althoff up to started at me blankly, evincing not even a dreg of familiarity with her work.

Her legions of followers cannot, in large part, be called “fans,” but do include avid viewers, reply guys, bewildered women, judgmental tradwives, hate-watchers, and pop culture fanatics. She collects connoisseurs more than disciples. As such, Althoff is a cipher, and a harbinger of a novel vector of celebrity that’s potentially liberating for women who’ve been trained to seek validation, adoration, and eternal “relevance,” as she puts it. This makes her an intriguingly modern economic actor. When she is recognized in public, she doesn’t tell her children that they just met a few of Mommy’s fans. “I say, these are all Mommy’s coworkers,” she tells me, seeming sincere as she emphasizes that she wouldn’t want her children to think she was traditionally “famous.” But she clearly can’t resist a facetious acknowledgment of how successful her campaign for relevance has been: “They think I have coworkers everywhere.”.

In a recent development, she “judges relevance by incoming brand deals,” which means she’s willing to maneuver to maintain your attention. “My audience has a lot of men who are just wishing they could see me naked,” she says, a reality she enthusiastically “manipulates a little bit.” She knows her combative approach to flirtation sparks outrage among her male viewers. She’s also aware that many of those men resort to infantile insults, which is where her deadpan self-deprecation comes in: “I want to beat people to the punch,” she claims. “You can't call me ugly and have it hurt me because I called myself ugly first. You can't say I'm not funny: I've already said it.”.

It has been revealed that when I relay to Althoff some of the questions my straight male friends had for her, she admits the rabid speculation around her sex life is frustrating but also flattering. “They obviously think I had a chance with these guests,” she deadpans. “There’s no interaction I can have with a man where people aren’t like, Oh, you guys fucked.” Her haters, she’s observed, fall into two camps: Trump voting white men “who think they would never have a chance with me” and believe unmarried mothers to be morally corrupt. On the flip side are “women who are jealous.”.

Recent findings suggest that her political leanings––which have veered far to the left since her childhood––periodically foment some turmoil among her newly introduced girl squad, but Althoff says she also finds much to admire in her conservative cast members lifestyles. “Do I agree with everything in the Church? No. But I see the beauty in the tradwife life.” The relationship between McCall DaPron, a fellow cast member and frenemy turned pseudo sister of Althoff’s, inspired her to break up with her ex, because she saw a healthy dynamic missing from her own relationship. She is committed to maintaining her conviction around political problems her cast members might rather not address: “Does it bother me when I’m the only one in the cast posting about certain things happening in the world? Yes. Fuck ICE, Free Palestine. Free Congo. Free Sudan.”.

It has been revealed that she hopes her onscreen proto-sister wives, and viewers like them, might allow her to “burst that bubble a little bit”—to widen their perspectives, open their eyes, and inspire re-evaluations of concerns close to Althoff’s heart. Admittedly, as the show illuminates, sometimes that means earnestly defending a political position, and other times it means (antifascistly?) refusing to follow the dress code one of the other women attempts to enforce at a party. Observing that male guests on her podcast “always rank themselves a ten out of ten, she notes that “men could be a little more realistic.” She’s not attacking all men, she clarifies, but she would like to alert them to the following: “I don't need to fuck every man that hits on me.”.

She adds, with the sprightly sarcasm that’s become her trademark, one final message to readers of this magazine: “Men who read GQ: be nicer to me. I’m not mean, I don’t hate you, don’t hate me.”.

Industry observers note that interiors, and interiority, are recurring subjects of Charlotte Eskildsen’s collections for The Garment. For pre-fall, the designer imagined a woman living in a townhouse in central Copenhagen near the Marble Church, a very chic area, who wears clothes in “her own really private way... Nothing in this collection is too tied up,” the designer stated. “Even if it’s suiting, it will stretch, and it’s comfortable to wear.”.

Some of the garments have a feeling of intimacy that comes from their origin in the boudoir. Lingerie dressing is a trend that Eskildsen isn’t ready to give up as she sees it as an expression of femininity that counters the outward strength often expected of women. So next to a lace-trimmed skirt with an asymmetrically inserted godet and a collarless jacket, the many slip dresses in the collection looked somewhat saccharine and less street-ready than the more structured looks. She’s “dressed, but she doesn’t know if she wants to go out or not,” the designer said of her muse. (This cozy, hazy should-I-or-shouldn’t-I feeling assumes win-win options.).

According to recent reports, in betweenness is at the heart of all pre-fall collections which need to adapt to snow and sun. For cooler temps there is a smart cropped black leather jacket shown with tailored white pants. An injection of romance comes in the form of a flowy Daisy Buchanan-ish dress the color of a snowflake with bias cut lines which combines silk chiffon, jacquard, and silk wool. There are “a lot of cut lines to be able to mix all the fabrics so it’s like a blanket of different fabrics,” as Eskildsen put it. Hygge, in other words, but make it haute.

Creamy Miso Mushroom Pasta

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mushroom fans: Bookmark this recipe immediately.
  • A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce.
  • Find more fall favorite meals here: Weeknight Pumpkin Chili; Cream-ish of Mushroom Soup; Mushrooms au Poivre.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mushroom fans: Bookmark this recipe immediately. It will give you everything you want when you crave a creamy mushroom pasta as soon as the crisp fall air sets in. The hardworking trio of miso, Parmesan, and touch of soy sauce delivers an umami bomb of flavor that doesn’t overwhelm, but magnifies, the best of earthy mushrooms. Coupled with luscious noodles enrobed in a creamy (but not heavy) sauce, what’s not to love?

A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce. The nests (Rummo and De Cecco are great accessible brands) cook far faster than standard straight pasta, almost as fast as fresh. (2) Don’t be afraid to season your mushrooms! Yes, I know this goes against all that we’ve learned about salting them too early in the cooking process, but just a bit of salt will get them going and releasing their water faster for eventual crisp-browned edges. Don’t be alarmed if you see a pool of water at the start of the mushroom cooking—that’s to be expected and just keep going until it evaporates. (3) Don’t forget to reserve plenty of pasta cooking liquid, which is critical to the eventual sauce’s success. I prefer transferring the al dente noodles from the pasta pot to the skillet, letting any residual water come with it (and to ensure you don’t accidentally drain away that liquid gold).

Find more fall favorite meals here: Weeknight Pumpkin Chili; Cream-ish of Mushroom Soup; Mushrooms au Poivre.

Cook 12 oz. egg-based pasta (such as fettuccine nests) in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally, until al dente, about 1 minute less than package directions.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over high. Add 1 lb. crimini or mixed mushrooms (such as button, maitake, oyster, and/or shiitake), sliced ¼" thick or torn into bite-size pieces, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and toss to coat evenly. Spread out into an even layer and cook, undisturbed, until mushrooms are starting to release their liquid, 2–3 minutes (do not be alarmed; there will be a lot). Continue to cook, tossing occasionally, until moisture is almost completely evaporated and edges of mushrooms are starting to brown, 6–8 minutes.

It has been revealed that reduce heat to medium-high; add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, tossing often, until garlic is fragrant and golden, 1–2 minutes. Pour in ¾ cup dry white wine, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan with a sturdy spatula or flat-edged wooden spoon, and cook until wine is mostly evaporated (you should have about 1 Tbsp. liquid left in pan), about 4 minutes. Reduce heat to medium-low. Add 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 2 Tbsp. white miso and stir until melted and combined. Slowly pour in ½ cup heavy cream, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan; simmer until thickened slightly, 2–3 minutes. Add 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce; season with freshly ground pepper. Taste and add more salt if needed.

According to recent reports, using tongs, transfer pasta to mushroom mixture and add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Increase heat to medium and bring to a simmer. Cook, tossing constantly and adding ½–1 cup more pasta cooking liquid to reach desired sauce consistency if needed, until pasta is al dente and liquid has thickened slightly, about 3 minutes.

Recent findings suggest that remove pan from heat. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup) to pasta and toss to combine. Season generously with more pepper; taste and season with more salt if needed.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan and pepper.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A decade ago, many of us wouldn’t leave the house without a full-coverage beat. As Instagram selfies and YouTube tutorials took over pop culture, meticulously sculpted, perfected complexions reigned supreme—until the pendulum swung in the opposite direction, ushering in an era of barely-there coverage and skin-care-infused formulas. And while the early 2020s were defined by ultra-dewy, almost damp-looking skin, today’s complexion ideal strikes a more nuanced balance: coverage without the weight, radiance without the shine.

According to recent reports, “Modern complexion formulations have come such a long way, and the new-Gen complexion products give medium to buildable coverage that glides and melts into skin, while giving a soft-focus matte finish that reads radiant rather than shiny,” indicates celebrity makeup artist and Vogue Beauty Board member Fara Homidi. “We can now get more coverage, while the final look is breathable and has flex to it, never heavy and cakey.” Nowadays, lightweight texture, skin-friendly ingredients, and flexible coverage are non-negotiable. The ideal product perfects your complexion without looking or feeling like makeup.

According to recent reports, “I want the complexion product to be able to be great, without the help of a concealer or bronzer,” says content creator and fellow Board member Toni Bravo. “It also needs the right undertones that bring out dimension naturally,” she says, to create a second-skin effect.

It has been revealed that mastering your complexion, however, is both the science of formulation and the art of application. While formulas are more advanced than ever, technique and placement have simultaneously evolved. Homidi points out that it’s not about wearing less makeup, but about how it’s placed on the skin. Her best advice is to put the product only where you need it like under the eyes or around the nose, with lighter coverage around the the rest of the face. She prefers pinpointing blemishes and discolorations with fuller coverage, while letting the rest of the skin breathe.

Industry observers note that looking ahead, beauty lovers and experts alike can expect complexion makeup to keep evolving. “Hopefully, complexion products continue to evolve shade-wise,” says Bravo. “We’ve seen brands truly expand the meaning of inclusivity in the last few years, in ways 14-year-old me wouldn’t believe. Folks understanding undertones, and how to apply them to our complexion products, will make for a more conscious consumer and intentional brand.” Meanwhile, Homidi expects further advancements in texture and innovative application methods (roller ball foundation applicator, anyone?). In short, the future looks more inclusive, with advanced formulations and better shade matches for everyone.

Below, a look at some of the latest foundation and skin tint launches that we believe are pushing the category forward; with some helpful insights from the Vogue Beauty Board members who have tested them.

Vogue Beauty Board’s Toni Bravo uses Dior’s Backstage Glow-Up Skin Tint.

According to recent reports, I love the glow and the wearability of this skin tint. I prefer a glowy finish, so this one was right up my alley. I have combination skin, so going forward I’d wear this with my favorite mattifying primer to keep it from getting too shiny. I used shade 8N. It pulls fairly neutral, so if you have a warmer undertone, I’d pay close attention to the swatches before applying, especially since it includes SPF.

FROM THE BOARD: Marianna Hewitt, beauty creator and Summer Fridays cofounder.

It has been revealed that “I love complexion products that still look like skin and what I like about this formula is the natural glow and the ability to build a little more coverage where you want it. It gives your skin a more even look without feeling overly heavy and perfect for light makeup days.”.

FROM THE BOARD: Conçetta Ciarlo, beauty shopping writer.

I was surprised by how much I liked this skin tint—I’m not usually fond of tints because they tend to look too shiny on my oily skin and don’t provide much coverage. The real draw here was the special attention to shades for neutral undertones (me!). I went with shade 2N, and it was a perfect match—plus, this gave a surprising amount of coverage, blurring away any light hyperpigmentation marks I had. The finish is definitely radiant, but I found it natural and lightweight-feeling. My only hesitation is that the formula isn’t totally non-comedogenic, and I’m acne-prone, so I’d reach for this when my skin is in maintenance mode (AKA clear, and upkeeping that) rather than actively breaking out.

FROM THE BOARD: Kiana Murden, beauty shopping editor.

First of all, I love that this is called a ‘tinted cream’—it feels like a modern reimagining of the tinted moisturizer. I tried this for the first time uptown at Violet Grey’s NYC boutique, and was so pleased with the shade match. I couldn’t believe how incredible my skin looked. When I got home, I put the tub front-and-center in my vanity (where I keep the things I reach for most often), and have used it for most makeup days since. Lightweight, sort of gel-like, and hydrating with a natural finish, this is a winner in my book.

Vogue Beauty Board’s Marianna Hewitt uses Carte Blanche’s Multi-Hyphenate.

FROM THE BOARD: Marianna Hewitt, beauty creator and Summer Fridays cofounder.

It has been revealed that I love formulas that bring skincare and makeup together in a thoughtful way. I like that this combines mineral SPF with brightening ingredients and it has a bit more coverage than a skin tint. This is perfect for mornings when you are in a rush and want to just apply one thing that combines multiple steps.

FROM THE BOARD: Kiana Murden, beauty shopping editor.

If you see me on a stage or at a photoshoot, this is probably the secret to my skin looking good. In fact, I’ve decided to leave it in my beauty closet makeup bag because I get ready for most weekday things from our office. Celebrity makeup artist Hung Vanngo’s serum foundation is easy to love. While many newer formulas are sheer or light coverage, this is medium-to-full. Fortunately it achieves such without the weight—blurring skin without feelign heavy, pilling, or caking. A feat!

Vogue Beauty Board’s Michelle Lee uses TIRTIR’s Tinted Skin Glow Cushion.

It has been revealed that I’m not typically a fan of cushion foundations. I’ve tried the other varieties of the TirTir cushion and never found one that I loved. I have very dry, dehydrated skin, so some cushions can accentuate dry spots, especially if there’s any peeling—but I really loved this one! The finish is dewy without looking oily, and the shade match (23N for me) was spot on. Another significant issue with cushions for me has always been the cleanliness of the puff, but I like this formulation so much, I’m committed to a regular puff-washing routine and getting extra puffs to have on hand.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that sit still for a second. The birds are singing. The sun is shining. The Air Jordan 4 ‘Bred’ is returning. Nature is healing. Everything, for once, is exactly where it should be.

The ‘Bred’ (short for “black and red”) is one of the original Air Jordan 4 colorways from 1989. Created by legendary Nike designer Tinker Hatfield, it came in slick black nubuck with hits of gray and red throughout. Michael Jordan famously wore a pair when he hit The Shot over Craig Ehlo to knock the Cleveland Cavaliers out of the 1989 NBA Playoffs—so, yeah, there’s a bit of lore there too.

Recent findings suggest that unsurprisingly, Jordan Brand has brought it back a few times over the past few years. There was a retro in 1999, followed by versions in 2008 and 2012, and then another in 2019, which finally brought the OG “Nike Air” branding back to the heel. Then, in 2024, we got the ‘Bred Reimagined,’ which swapped the classic nubuck for leather. The less stated about that one, the better.

Because two years later, Jordan Brand is going back to the good stuff. The ‘Bred’ is decked out in black nubuck again, with gray eyelets, red accents around the sole, and the all-notable “Nike Air” stamped across the back. Even the Nike branding on the outsole is returning. Basically, if you looked at the ‘Bred Reimagined’ and thought, “Look how they massacred my boy,” congrats: this one's for you.

And there’s something quite nice about that. The AJ4 has been messed with, remixed, collabed on, and reworked in just about every way possible over the last few years. Some of those experiments have been great! Some… not so much. The ‘Bred’ doesn’t really need any of that. It’s been one of the best Air Jordans on the planet for 37 years. If it ain’t broke, don’t fix it.

The Air Jordan 4 ‘Bred’ is set to drop on November 27 via Nike, the SNKRS app, and select stockists globally.

Hot tip: Make sure to shake the cocktail for a good 20 seconds or more to get it homogeneous and frothy. This is the secret to getting a smooth drink without any curdling or separation. I haven’t made a meal in the French countryside in fall; but sometimes I dream, and these slow-cooked lentils are what I’d make in such a situation. Back in my American reality, it still makes an excellent dinner or hearty weekend lunch. Look for mild smoked Austrian or German sausages, which lean on mellow herbs and warm spices (sometimes, if you’re lucky, they’re also stuffed with a nutty cheese)—this style is already cooked to a safe temperature, but the casing’s texture is greatly improved when seared before reheating. If your shop only carries sweet Italian sausage or something like an apple-stuffed chicken sausage, both work in a pinch. What a treat it will be to actually finish off that gallon of apple cider you impulsively bought last week in the lentil-braising liquid.

More great fall recipes this way: Charred Cabbage With Sausages and Apples; Pork Chops With Green Chiles and Apples; Mustardy Cider-Braised Pork Chops.

According to recent reports, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 6–8 smoked Austrian or German sausages (1–1½ lb.), turning often, until deeply browned on all sides, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a plate.

Combine 1 large red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 3 celery stalks, finely chopped, 1 large carrot, peeled, finely chopped, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in same pan. Reduce heat to medium and cook, stirring often and scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan, until vegetables are softened, 6–8 minutes. Add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and cook, stirring, just until fragrant, about 1 minute.

In a recent development, add 2 cups low-sodium chicken or vegetable broth, 1½ cups apple cider, 1½ cups French green lentils, picked through, rinsed, ½ cup finely chopped parsley, 3 Tbsp. Dijon or whole grain mustard, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to pan. Increase heat to high and bring to a boil. Cook until liquid is slightly reduced, about 5 minutes. Cover pan, reduce heat to medium-low, and cook until lentils are tender and most of the liquid is absorbed but mixture is still saucy, 30–35 minutes.

Uncover pan and stir in 1 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar or red wine vinegar. Nestle sausages into lentil mixture and add any juices pooled on plate. Simmer until sausages are warmed through, about 5 minutes. Top with parsley leaves and reserved celery leaves to serve.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, over the last few years, lymphatic drainage has gone from an IYKYK technique to an all-out wellness obsession. Oft described as the “Cinderella of medicine,” the lymphatic system is responsible for collecting excess fluid from tissues, transporting immune cells, and carrying certain waste products away from cells. This system, however, doesn’t work on its own to get the lymph flowing. Lymphatic drainage is a more manual practice; you can try your hand at deep breathing or dry brushing, but few things offer offer as excellent lifting benefits as the best gua sha tools.

“The literal gua sha Mandarin translation is ‘to scrape sand,’” explains Lin Chen, cofounder of Pink Moon. “Gua sha tools have been used as a unique approach for holistic healing in China for 4,000 years. It has been traditionally used over the body to help aid in the movement of qi (which is energy flow), increase circulation, and release tension.” That stated, Chen continues saying that research indicates that the practice was first used in the Paleolithic Ages, dating back to the Ming dynasty in China.

Industry observers note that “Gua sha is an effective technique for enhancing the face’s natural contours and reducing puffiness through lymphatic drainage,” explains Charlotte Yau, traditional Chinese medicine expert and founder of Muihood. The upward-scraping technique is meant to stimulate blood circulation, encourage collagen production, and reduce the appearance of fine lines and wrinkles, adds Yau. “While it doesn’t permanently change facial structure, it can create a more sculpted look over time by reducing fluid retention and enhancing skin elasticity.”.

According to recent reports, of course, when you’re shopping for your first one, the options can feel endless. “When choosing a gua sha, I think the material, shape and weight all matter,” says Ava Lee, K-beauty expert and founder of byAVA. Ceramic and stone feel smooth and give you a gentler massage, while stainless steel stays cold, which helps with puffiness. “Ultimately, it’s about finding something that feels good to use and that you’ll reach for every day,” Lee says. Ahead, the best gua sha tools to add to your routine from Lanshin, Wildling, and more.

What are the benefits of incorporating a gua sha tool?

“While its popularity in the US and Europe is largely tied to its ability to ‘sculpt’ the face, its healing capabilities extend far deeper!” Chen instructs, explaining that the gua sha is used for lymphatic drainage, addressing stagnant energy, promoting blood flow, soothing headaches, reducing inflammation, shortening acute illnesses like colds and flus, as well as releasing tension from head to toe. Daily gua sha practice has the ability to enhance not only your appearance (think reduced puffiness, contoured facial muscles, and improved skin elasticity), but your mental and emotional well-being. Just think of how calming it is to glide a roller or stone across your skin. What’s more, Chen indicates you can expect results instantly, though you should continue to use daily.

“Both steel and stone gua sha tools have their benefits, and the choice depends on personal preference and skin needs,” explains Chinese Medicine expert and founder of Muihood, Charlotte Yau.

Curious how to use a gua sha? So you’re ready to try the restorative practice at home. Aside from the tool you choose, a proper technique is key to reap the anticipated benefits. Always start with clean skin, then prep with an emollient face oil or balm. “You also want to apply an oil that’s silky and doesn’t absorb right away or you might tug your skin,” Chen advises. With skin ready, keep the stone as flat and close to the skin as possible, gliding at a 15 degree angle to avoid any unnecessary friction. According to Chen, you’ll want to avoid passing over active breakouts, even if you just target the chest and neck to increase circulation and decrease inflammation. Perform slow strokes, in upward and outward motions, for about three to five passes, and you’re all set.

In a recent development, yau recommends starting from the neck and moving upward to the jawline, cheeks, and forehead to promote proper lymphatic drainage. “For best results, use your gua sha three to five times per week. Daily use can enhance benefits, but overuse may cause sensitivity,” she says. After each use, Yau says it’s key to cleanse tools with warm water and soap to prevent bacteria build-up and unnecessary breakouts.

Mistakes To Avoid When Using a Gua Sha.
